meta.title: Crochet Plushie Business Dashboard
meta.notes: Source data compiled via research through July 2026. Re-verify time-sensitive figures (postage rates, platform pricing, unconfirmed convention dates) periodically. Convention cost/barrier-to-entry data added 2026-07-10 via vendor-page research -- many table costs are gated behind an application step and could not be confirmed publicly; re-verify directly with organizers before budgeting. Product-demand research (bestsellers, price clustering, bundling, under-represented items) added 2026-07-10 -- mostly craft-business blog consensus rather than raw sales data; several items are flagged as single-source or outright data gaps.

copyrightNotes.lovecraftSpecific: Most Lovecraft stories are public domain in the US (never renewed, or pre-1929). The Cthulhu Mythos was an intentionally 'open' shared universe from the start. Generic tentacled elder-god designs based on text descriptions are safe; copying a specific illustrator's or game company's distinctive rendering is not.

conventionRankings.caveat: Most convention vendor pricing is gated behind an application step rather than posted publicly, even for major events (Anime Expo, SDCC, WonderCon, L.A. Comic Con). Treat "not publicly posted" entries as needing direct outreach before budgeting.

bestsellers.finding: Small/quick amigurumi under ~4in (mushrooms, mini bears, strawberries, ghosts, donuts) consistently outsell larger, detailed pieces at in-person events -- shoppers buy them on impulse.
Keychains/mini charms are fast-selling, low-yarn, low-risk items that often serve as a booth 'entry point' drawing buyers in before bigger purchases.
Animal designs (octopus, axolotl, cats, dogs, bears, turtles) and food-shaped items are named most often as reliable bestsellers, ahead of niche fandom pieces.
Medium-size plushies ($20-$50) are the format kids gravitate to for play value (e.g. snuggle dragons), distinct from keychains bought as impulse/gift items.
Sellers explicitly prioritize fast-to-make items over highly detailed pieces for craft-fair viability -- a supply-side signal (seller convenience), not direct proof of lower demand for large pieces.

priceRange.finding: $10-$25 is repeatedly identified as the core impulse-buy range at craft fairs/conventions for keychains, small plushies, and similar giftable items.
One source frames $25-$50 (not $20) as where most sales likely live, reserving $10-$20 for the smallest impulse items only.
Two-tier pricing pattern reported: mini amigurumi/keychains cluster at $8-$18; medium plushies with safety eyes cluster at $20-$35.
'$20 and under' is explicitly and repeatedly used as vendor shorthand for the psychological impulse-buy threshold, though no hard sales data was cited by any source.
New/beginner vendors are advised to start at $5-$10/item before working up to a $20-25/hour-of-labor pricing target used by more experienced sellers.

bundles.finding: '3 for $X' bundle pricing (e.g. 3-for-$18, 3-for-$25) is recommended across multiple sources as a way to move small plushies/keychains faster and pair slow movers with bestsellers.
'Buy 2 get 1 free' deals are cited as a top performer by one vendor account -- but in jewelry, not plushies, so treat as an adjacent-craft signal only.
Mystery bags/blind-box plushies are a well-established, actively sold format on Etsy specifically for crochet plushies, typically bundling 2-3 plushies to meet or exceed the paid value.
Mystery/grab bags appear tied to TikTok 'gacha'/'lucky box' trends -- popularity may be partly social-media-aesthetic-driven rather than pure value-seeking.
No source quantifies bundling as a percentage of total sales for finished plushies -- only qualitative "bundles increase average transaction size" claims exist.

gaps.finding: Skin-tone yarn availability is a documented pain point among crafters, prompting creation of a dedicated 8-shade skin-tone yarn line -- maker-side evidence is stronger than confirmed end-customer demand.
Custom/made-to-order plushies show demand signals via active seller waitlists (explicit 'There is a Waitlist!' listings), suggesting custom capacity is a bottleneck for at least some shops.
Allergen/hypoallergenic material guidance appears mainly as seller-side safety advice, not documented buyer complaints -- currently a data gap, not a confirmed underserved niche.
No direct evidence found on size-option gaps, LGBTQ+ representation, or adult/collector positioning via Reddit/TikTok searches -- flagged as a genuine research gap, not a "no demand" finding.
gaps.source: N/A -- recommend a manual Reddit/TikTok search pass if decision-critical

yarnBrands.finding: Chenille/blanket-style yarn is the dominant category for sellable plushies; in a 7-yarn side-by-side maker test, Hobbii Baby Snuggle rated softest and easiest to work with, while Bernat Blanket rated firmest (best for shape retention).

Premier Parfait Chunky and Hobbii Baby Snuggle are treated as near-interchangeable substitutes by plushie makers on TikTok (same thickness, overlapping colors) -- useful backup when one is out of stock.

Among standard acrylics, Red Heart Super Saver (cheapest, widest colors, scratchy), Caron Simply Soft (softer but splitty), and Hobby Lobby I Love This Yarn recur most in Reddit comparisons -- consensus is all three work and choice is preference-driven.
WeCrochet/Knit Picks Brava (worsted/sport) is a frequently blogged best-value amigurumi acrylic: soft, durable, machine-washable, huge palette including skin tones, ~$2.49-2.99/skein.
For cotton, Paintbox Cotton DK (~$2-3/skein, big palette) appears in best-amigurumi-yarn roundups; no strong amigurumi-specific ranking found for Lion Brand 24/7 Cotton or Scheepjes Catona.

yarnPricing.finding: Bernat Blanket (10.5oz/220yd): Walmart 6-pack listed at $19.99 (~$3.33/skein, ~1.5 cents/yd) but other Walmart listings show ~$9.50/skein -- pricing varies wildly by listing; multipacks are generally the cheapest route. Verify at checkout.
Premier Parfait Chunky (3.5oz/131yd): $5.49/skein direct from Premier (~4.2 cents/yd); Michaels marketplace listings run $9.78-14.34 -- buy direct or Walmart, not Michaels marketplace.
Hobbii Honey Bunny: $9.60/skein at 1-3 units with quantity discounts at higher counts; Hobbii Baby Snuggle ~$8.80/skein (2024 observation).
WeCrochet Brava Worsted: $2.49/skein for 218yd (~1.1 cents/yd) -- among the cheapest quality acrylics available.

Joann is gone: all ~790 stores liquidated by May 30, 2025. Michaels acquired Joann's IP and private labels (e.g. Big Twist). Practical channels now: Michaels, Hobby Lobby, Walmart, and direct online (Yarnspirations, Hobbii, Crochet.com).

qualityReputation.finding: Bernat Blanket (current yarn): praised for firmness/shape retention, but documented complaints of skein-to-skein color-run and tension inconsistency even within the same dye lot, plus a long official discontinued-shades list (9 standard + 58 Blanket Big) -- a real color-continuity risk for a fixed product line.

Chenille/velvet yarns generally (incl. Bernat Velvet): worming (loops popping out of finished fabric) and shedding are the most-cited issues; standard fix is smaller hooks and tighter tension. Yarn ends are prone to wiggling loose in amigurumi.
Caron Simply Soft is frequently criticized for splitting during tight amigurumi stitches; Red Heart Super Saver is durable and cheap but scratchy for a premium plushie feel.
Hobbii Baby Snuggle/Honey Bunny praised as softest with strong cores; one maker warns Hobbii's newer 'Toucan' chenille has a weaker inner thread (single-source anecdote).
WeCrochet Brava reviewers report it 'never feels cheap' with good stitch definition and durability -- few complaints found.

bulkWholesale.finding: Yarnspirations has a formal wholesale program (contact form) plus retail tiered promos ('Buy 3-4, get 10% off') and clearance up to 60% -- the most direct wholesale path for Bernat Blanket.
Hobbii has no published wholesale program but offers built-in quantity discounts (e.g. Honey Bunny cheaper at 4+ skeins), color-pack bundles, 50%-off sale collections, and free US shipping at $75+.
Walmart multipacks (6- and 10-pack Bernat Blanket) are effectively the cheapest bulk channel without a wholesale account, though listing prices are inconsistent.
WeCrochet Brava functions as a de facto bulk value line (~1.1 cents/yd retail, no minimums). True wholesale minimum-order details for Hobbii or LoveCrafts: not found.

eyesAndStuffing.finding: 6060eyes.com (18+ year amigurumi specialist) sells bulk safety-eye packs (e.g. 25 pairs of 6mm solid black, typical small packs ~$1.50-2.85), US child-safety compliant. Note: their Etsy store was suspended March 2024 -- they now sell only via their own site.
GlassEyesOnline is a wholesale-oriented supplier of safety eyes/noses in all sizes (listings from ~$6) -- good for odd sizes and animal noses.

Fairfield Poly-Fil Premium 10lb box is the standard business-scale stuffing; reviewers cite Walmart as ~20% cheaper than other channels (eBay listing ~$74.70, 2025-26; Walmart typically notably less -- exact current price unconfirmed).

etsyFees.finding: Listing fee is $0.20 per listing, charged at creation and each 4-month renewal whether it sells or not.
Transaction fee is 6.5% of total order value including shipping/gift wrap; US payment processing (Etsy Payments) adds 3% + $0.25 per order.
Offsite Ads: 15% on ad-attributed orders if trailing-12-month sales are under $10,000 (can opt out); drops to 12% but becomes mandatory once you cross $10,000.
One-time shop setup fee of roughly $15-$29 for new shops (introduced Sept 2024). No US Regulatory Operating Fee exists (that fee applies only in certain countries, e.g. Canada 1.15%, UK 0.32%).
etsyFees.source: craftybase.com (2026; setup-fee range varies by source)

etsyFees.finding: Illustrative $25 plushie sale (free shipping, no offsite ad): $0.20 listing + $1.63 transaction + $1.00 processing = $2.83 (~11.3% all-in). If offsite-ad-attributed at 15%, add $3.75 for $6.58 total (~26.3%).
etsyFees.source: Arithmetic on verified 2026 rates; Etsy official fee page returned 403 so figures rest on consistent secondary sources

paymentProcessing.finding: Square: 2.6% + $0.15 per tap/dip/swipe on the free plan (raised from +$0.10 in the Oct 2025 pricing overhaul -- older sources showing 10 cents are outdated); contactless+chip reader $59; no monthly fee.
PayPal Zettle (now 'PayPal POS'): 2.29% + $0.09 in-person -- cheapest per-transaction card rate of the group; first reader $29 ($79 after); no monthly fee.
Venmo business profile: 1.9% + $0.10 on standard in-app QR payments -- cheapest option overall. Tap to Pay card rates conflict across sources (2.29% + $0.10 vs 2.9% + $0.09) -- verify in-app.
paymentProcessing.confidence: High (QR rate); Low (Tap to Pay rate)

paymentProcessing.finding: SumUp US: 2.6% + $0.10 in-person, reader ~$39-$54, no monthly fee (one craft-fair guide cites 2.75% -- US pricing pages vary).
Shopify POS is generally not worth it for a fair-only seller -- competitive in-person rates require a paid plan (~$128/month on Basic with POS Pro); only makes sense with an existing Shopify store.

Square is the most-used reader among handmade sellers per craft-fair guides (free app, easy setup, inventory tracking, next-day deposits); in practice most vendors offer Square/Zettle plus a Venmo QR code.

boothStartup.finding: Indoor artist-alley minimal kit (floor-length tablecloth, small risers, price signs, card reader) can be done for under ~$100 excluding banner; a vertical banner and gridwall panels are the usual first upgrades.

Consensus artist-alley checklist: floor-length table cover (hides storage), gridwall/wire displays for vertical space, large clear price signage, name banner, business cards, cash box, battery lighting.
Outdoor 10x10 pop-up canopy: budget models ~$80-$200, vendor-grade commercial frames $200-$400, custom-printed $400-$1,000+; weights add $50-$100.
Plan roughly 40lb of weight per canopy leg since staking is usually banned (some events require 25lb/leg); sidewalls are a recommended add-on for wind/sun control.
boothStartup.confidence: High (recommendation); the 40lb figure is one guide's rule of thumb

boothStartup.finding: Rough startup totals: indoor table budget setup ~$100-$250, mid-tier with banner + gridwall + lighting ~$300-$600; outdoor Ren-Faire booth budget ~$350-$600, mid-tier ~$800-$1,500. Ranges assembled from component prices, not a single sourced total.
Budget the booth fee itself at +20-30% over the headline fee for true event cost (parking, electricity, insurance riders).

pricingFormulas.finding: Formula A (most-cited for crochet): Price = (Materials + Time x Hourly Rate) x 2.0-2.5 markup.

Formula B (classic wholesale/retail): (Materials + Labor + Overhead) = base; base x2 = wholesale; wholesale x2 = retail (i.e. cost x4 retail). Overhead commonly estimated at 15-25% of materials + labor.
Formula C (Made Urban variant): (Materials x 2) + Labor + Overhead = wholesale, x2 = retail.
Hourly-rate benchmark corroborated: $15-25/hr general floor, $12-15 beginner, $15-25 intermediate, $25-40 advanced; amigurumi-specific guides use $20/hr in worked examples.

Known amigurumi tension: full formulas on slow-to-make plushies produce prices the market resists (a worked example prices an 8-hour elephant at $195). A $25 plushie only supports ~30-45 min of paid labor under Formula A -- guides recommend faster patterns or accepting some unpaid labor rather than lowering the hourly rate.

marketingChannels.finding: Hard, corroborated data comparing TikTok vs Instagram vs Etsy-search conversion for crochet plushie sellers specifically does not exist -- the evidence base is almost entirely anecdote.
marketingChannels.confidence: High (that this is the state of evidence)

marketingChannels.finding: Viral-TikTok anecdotes exist (2M+ views producing 400+ orders; 50k followers in 3 months leading to sell-out drops) but read like content-mill composites with no named/verifiable shops -- treat as illustrative only.

A genuine primary-source testimonial exists: a January 2026 YouTube '2025 Crochet Recap' where one plushie seller breaks down markets-vs-Etsy numbers (plushies sold, fees compared) -- worth watching directly.

Craft-business guides consistently report in-person craft fairs/markets as the strongest-converting channel for plushies (buyers can touch the item, no shipping friction), with Etsy as year-round baseline and social media as the discovery layer feeding both.
TikTok-to-Etsy crossover is observable: Etsy hosts dedicated 'viral TikTok crochet' market pages, indicating TikTok trends measurably drive Etsy search demand for plushies.

legal.finding: CDTFA seller's permit is required to sell taxable goods at CA conventions/craft fairs: a free temporary permit covers selling under 90 days, but doing 3+ events in 12 months requires a regular (permanent) permit -- also free. Obtain up to 90 days before the event via CDTFA online, registering each event location.
Event operators are required to verify vendor permits (typically via form CDTFA-410-D), and most convention vendor applications ask for your permit number.

Sales tax rate is the rate where the event is held: 7.25% statewide base plus district taxes (LA County venues run ~9.5%+). The vendor collects and remits on their own CDTFA return -- conventions do not remit for you. Use the CDTFA address-based rate lookup per venue.
legal.source: cdtfa.ca.gov district-tax page; taxjar.com festival guide

legal.finding: Liability insurance: Ren faires and larger conventions commonly require a certificate of insurance naming the event/venue as additional insured; small comic cons often do not. Typical craft-vendor cost: ACT Insurance from ~$49/event or ~$279/year; FLIP from ~$299/year (industry range $40-60/event, $200-400/year).

CPSIA: handmade plushies marketed to children 12-and-under are 'children's products' requiring third-party testing at a CPSC-accepted lab (ASTM F963), a Children's Product Certificate, and a permanent tracking label.

The CPSC Small Batch Manufacturer registry (free, annual; under ~$1.48M revenue and 7,500 units) waives most third-party testing but NOT lead-in-substrate rules -- and a CPC and tracking label are still required.

A 'not intended for children under 3' tag is NOT a reliable shield: CPSC classifies by overall design, marketing, and appeal -- a cute plushie displayed at a con will likely be deemed a children's product regardless of disclaimer. Adult/collector positioning only works if design and marketing genuinely target adults.
Several states require stuffed-article 'law tags'/registry numbers (e.g. Pennsylvania URN, honored by reciprocity in other states).
